title: Sorted List With Express Lanes
statement:
Build a skip list: a sorted linked list with extra "express lanes" stacked on top. The bottom lane links every value in order. Each lane above links a random subset of the lane below, so a search can race along a high lane, drop down, and race again, much like taking an express train and then a local one.

  • SkipList() creates an empty list.
  • search(target) returns true if target is stored at least once.
  • add(num) stores num. Duplicates are allowed and each copy counts separately.
  • erase(num) removes one copy of num and returns true, or returns false if num is not stored.

Each operation should take O(log n) time on average. Do not lean on a built-in sorted container: the point is to build the lanes yourself.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first creates the list. The expected output has one entry per operation (null where nothing is returned). The random lane heights never change the outputs.

examples.out: [null, null, null, null, false, null, true, false, true, false]
examples.why: 4 is missing until it is added. Erasing 9, which was never added, returns false and changes nothing.

examples.out: [null, null, null, true, true, true, false]
examples.why: Two copies of 7. Erasing removes only one, so 7 is still found until the second erase.

hints: A sorted linked list makes search O(n) because you must step through every node. What if some nodes also had a link that jumps far ahead?
Give each new node a random height: level 1 always, level 2 with probability 1/2, level 3 with 1/4, and so on. Each node keeps one next pointer per level.

Search from the top level of a head sentinel: move right while the next value is smaller than the target, then drop a level. Record the last node at each level; add and erase splice in or out right after those nodes.

explain.intuition:
Binary search needs random access, which a linked list lacks. A skip list fakes it with lanes. Level 1 is the full sorted list. About half of the nodes also appear on level 2, a quarter on level 3, and so on. Searching from the top, each lane skips about half of what is left below it, so the walk is O(log n) steps on average, like halving a range.

The random heights are what keep it balanced without any rotations like a balanced tree needs. Insertion just flips coins for the new node's height. Every operation starts with the same walk: go right while the next value is smaller, then drop down. The node where you dropped on each level is exactly where a new node gets linked in, or an old one gets unlinked.
steps: Use a head sentinel with the maximum number of levels (16 is plenty for 50 000 items). Each node has val and an array next, one pointer per level.
Walk: from the top level down, move right while cur.next[lvl].val < num, and record prev[lvl] = cur before dropping.
search: after the walk, check whether prev[0].next[0] holds target.
add: pick a height by flipping coins, create the node, and for each level below its height link it right after prev[lvl].
erase: if the node after prev[0] holds num, unlink that node from every level where prev[lvl].next[lvl] is it. Return whether one was found.
pitfalls: Moving right while the next value is ≤ num. Then the walk skips past the copies, and erase cannot find the node to remove.
On erase, unlinking whatever node follows prev[lvl] on each level instead of only the node being removed. With duplicates those can be different nodes.
Giving every node full height, which turns it back into a slow list with extra pointers.

solutions.title: Sorted array with binary search
solutions.idea: Keep a sorted array. Binary search finds positions in O(log n); inserting or removing shifts the elements after it, which is O(n) but fast in practice. Good as a baseline, not what the question asks for.
solutions.time: O(log n) search, O(n) add and erase

solutions.title: Real skip list
solutions.idea: A head sentinel with 16 levels and nodes of random height. One shared walk finds the last node before num on every level; search, add and erase all build on it.

followups: Add rank(num): how many stored values are smaller than num. What would each link need to store?
Why do databases such as Redis use skip lists for sorted sets instead of balanced trees?
Make it safe for many concurrent readers and writers. Why is a skip list easier to lock than a tree?
